input.question: Low earth orbit speed is 15,430 mph to 17,450 mph. Escape speed must be higher. Why did it take Apollo missions three days to reach the moon, then, when it is only ~238,900 miles away?
input.ground_truth: Remember [Kepler's 2nd Law](_URL_1_) - orbits sweep out equal areas in equal time. For an elliptical orbit, such as a transfer orbit to the Moon, the effect of this law is that as you get further from Earth, the distance traveled along your orbit in a given time is less. So as the Apollo missions were traveling out to the Moon, they were constantly slowing down the entire time. By the time they were close enough to the Moon for the Moon's gravity to start pulling them inwards, [they were only traveling about 1113m/s](_URL_0_), or 2,489 mph.

Question: Low earth orbit speed is 15,430 mph to 17,450 mph. Escape speed must be higher. Why did it take Apollo missions three days to reach the moon, then, when it is only ~238,900 miles away?

response.prediction:
Okay, let’s imagine you have a really fast toy car, and you want to send it to your friend who lives far away.

Even if your car goes really fast—like super, super fast—just going straight to your friend’s house isn’t always the best way. If you just point your car straight at your friend’s house and go as fast as you can, you might miss and go past, or not have enough power to get all the way there.

Going to the Moon is a bit like that. The Earth is kind of like a big hill that pulls things toward it with gravity. If you just go really fast straight at the Moon, you might not have enough speed to escape the Earth’s pull, or you might not go in exactly the right direction.

So, the rocket going to the Moon doesn’t just go straight there as fast as it can. Instead, it goes around the Earth a few times in a big circle (that’s called an “orbit”), and then it carefully points itself toward the Moon and uses its engines to get there. It also needs to go the right speed so it doesn’t fall back to Earth or fly past the Moon.

That’s why it takes a few days—because the rocket doesn’t just zoom straight to the Moon. It follows a special path, kind of like taking a curvy road instead of a straight line, and it goes step by step to make sure it gets there safely.

So, even though the Moon is close, the rocket takes its time to make sure it gets there just right!
